value.reason: It captures and replays the v2 incident, but never ties the known-failure baseline's candidate to the claimed intended predecessor and broadly tolerates candidate drift. Its manual generation-11 check duplicates only part of the existing generation validator, leaving archived evidence validation incomplete.
The new capture and lineage entry points raise not-implemented errors, while the overlay arguments are ignored. Existing validation is left intact, but the requested recovery is absent.

It uses the existing live-binding checks and a shared byte overlay, but never proves that the baseline candidate is the intended predecessor. Its historical candidate and path-drift exemptions can therefore accept an unrelated baseline, weakening the new incident's proof.

It joins the baseline candidate to the intended predecessor and dispatches the v2 lifecycle while retaining v1 defaults. Some nested subject-manifest reads omit the overlay and committed-fallback arguments, so archived evidence can be read from the live path and the parallel file-resolution path is incomplete.

It revalidates archived generation evidence through the shared validators, but never ties the baseline candidate to the intended predecessor and suppresses historical candidate drift for that unjoined record. Its separate generation-11 parser duplicates validation logic and leaves the new proof narrower than claimed.

It derives and binds the predecessor lineage, dispatches the schemas, and reopens archived evidence through the existing validators. Apply and postvalidate omit the incident and disposition outputs from their outside-status comparison, so a valid migration is rejected when either output remains untracked after the reviews are committed.

Historical candidate drift inside a bound broad outcome becomes a nested bound_record_invalid issue, which its incident check does not tolerate, so the intended capture cannot validate ordinary historical evidence. When that drift occurs, it also skips bound validation of the owner attestation, weakening the new lifecycle proof despite its schema routing and overlay support.

It wires exact replay and archived generation and review validation through shared mechanisms while preserving the v1 defaults. The incident never checks that its caller-supplied intended predecessor equals the known-failure baseline's candidate HEAD and tree, so it can accept a lineage unrelated to the predecessor that actually invalidated the adopted attempt.

The new lineage, incident, and capture functions are stubs, with no v2 dispatch or replay. Validate-generation accepts overlay arguments but ignores them, making the new validation interface appear to verify relocated bytes when it only reads the live workspace.

Its historical baseline check filters candidate drift only at the outer level, while nested broad-outcome validation returns bound_record_invalid for that drift; normal invalidated evidence is therefore rejected. It also checks owner and pending attestation shape without reopening their full bound contracts, leaving the new adoption guarantee weaker even though v1 remains routed separately.

The incident requires the known-failure candidate HEAD to equal the intended predecessor, although this recovery's candidate was captured at the older workspace-baseline HEAD; the intended case is therefore rejected. It adds the right schema and replay machinery in the migration layer, but its special historical validation also bypasses a ledger future-absence check.

It implements the incident, v2 dispatch, row-exact replay, and validator overlay, but historical validation suppresses candidate Git identity and path-set failures without proving that the candidate belongs to the frozen workspace and predecessor lineage. The scoped overlay reuses validators, while its broad exception to their candidate checks and an ignored output path edge case leave real concerns.

It derives a Git-backed lineage and validates adopted evidence through the existing generation and review paths, but v2 accepts only complete pre-move or post-move states. A crash after one archive row is published makes the next apply reject the exact intermediate state, so the required crash-safe replay is absent.

It supports partial row replay and routes the overlay into the established validators, but its historical candidate path suppresses Git identity failures wholesale and treats any clean landing at current HEAD as sufficient, even outside the frozen predecessor range. The separate read-policy and view machinery adds a parallel layer, and apply does not require the incident to be committed.

The incident and overlay cover the reported predecessor mismatch, but v2 rejects every partially moved state before apply can resume. Its historical evidence check also discards candidate path-set drift broadly, so the new path weakens a validation guarantee instead of proving each allowed change.

The incident, lineage, and capture functions only raise not-implemented errors, and the new generation overlay parameters are accepted but ignored. The CLI and exports advertise a recovery that cannot run; no schema-dispatched replay or archived evidence validation exists.

It derives the first-parent projection from Git, binds owner facts and attempt rows, and reopens partially relocated evidence through the existing validators for exact replay. Its historical candidate scope no longer checks the original index digest and permits extra observed dirty paths, while a lone malformed Retirement-Transaction-ID marker is classified as uncovered rather than rejected.

The incident and v2 evidence path are present, but its adopted view demands either every source row or a complete archive; one hard-linked archive row after a crash prevents apply from resuming. The historical baseline path also drops candidate path-set mismatch checks broadly, leaving the established validation weaker in this recovery.
